concepts.title: Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)
concepts.one_liner: Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) are architectures for sequential computation that use feedback connections to create cycles in their computation graphs.
concepts.content: RNNs are a neural net architecture for modeling sequences, performing sequential rather than parallel computation. Unlike feedforward architectures represented by directed acyclical computation graphs, RNNs are neural nets with feedback connections. A feedback connection defines a recurrence in the computational graph, meaning the outputs of one layer can send a message back to earlier in the computational pipeline. To make this well-defined, RNNs introduce the notion of a timestep, where one timestep corresponds to one functional call to each layer, mapping that layer's inputs to its outputs. (see figure: Basic RNN with one hidden layer.) (see figure: RNN with multidimensional inputs, hidden states, and outputs.)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard feedforward networks are limited to fixed-size inputs and outputs; RNNs solve this by using internal state to process sequences of arbitrary length.
concepts.recap_md: - RNNs use feedback connections to process sequential data through time.

concepts.title: Recurrent Layer
concepts.one_liner: A recurrent layer uses a state variable to maintain memory, updating its state based on current input and previous state to produce an output.
concepts.content: A recurrent layer is defined by the following equations: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{h}_t &= f(\mathbf{h}_{t-1}, \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[t]) &\triangleleft \quad\quad \text{update state based on input and previous state}\\ \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}[t]&= g(\mathbf{h}_t) &\triangleleft \quad\quad \text{produce output based on state} \end{aligned}$$ This is a layer that includes a state variable, $\mathbf{h}$. The operation of the layer depends on its state, and the layer updates its state every time it is called; therefore, the state acts as a kind of memory.
concepts.motivation_md: Recurrent layers allow a network to maintain information about previous inputs, enabling the model to learn dependencies across time in sequential data.
concepts.recap_md: - The hidden state $\mathbf{h}_t$ acts as a memory that is updated at each timestep.

concepts.title: Simple Recurrent Network (SRN)
concepts.one_liner: A Simple Recurrent Network (SRN) is a recurrent layer where the state update and output are computed using linear layers followed by pointwise nonlinearities.
concepts.content: One common kind of recurrent layer is the Simple Recurrent Network (SRN), defined by Elman. For this layer, $f$ is a linear layer followed by a pointwise nonlinearity, and $g$ is another linear layer. The full computation is defined by the following equations: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{h}_t &= \sigma_1(\mathbf{W}\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{U}\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[t]+ \mathbf{b})\\ \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}[t]&= \sigma_2(\mathbf{V}\mathbf{h}_t + \mathbf{c}) \end{aligned}$$ where $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ are pointwise nonlinearities. In SRNs, tanh is the common choice for the nonlinearity, but ReLUs and other choices may also be used.
concepts.motivation_md: SRNs provide a basic framework for capturing temporal patterns by combining current inputs with a linear transformation of the previous hidden state.
concepts.recap_md: - SRNs update the hidden state using a linear combination of the previous state and current input.

concepts.title: Backpropagation through Time (BPTT)
concepts.one_liner: Backpropagation through Time (BPTT) is a technique for training RNNs by unrolling them into a directed acyclic graph over a fixed number of timesteps.
concepts.content: Backpropagation is only defined for DAGs, and since RNNs are not DAGs, we apply backpropagation by unrolling the net for $T$ timesteps. This creates a DAG representation of the truncated RNN, known as Backpropagation through Time (BPTT). This approach yields exact gradients when $T$ equals the total number of timesteps; otherwise, it is an approximation that ignores dependencies longer than $T$. (see figure: Backpropagation through time in an RNN.) For a total cost $J$ summed over losses at each timestep, the gradient is: $$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial J}{\partial [\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{U}, \mathbf{V}]} = \sum_{t=0}^T \frac{\partial \mathcal{L}(\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}[t], \mathbf{y}_t)}{\partial [\mathbf{W}, \mathbf{U}, \mathbf{V}]} \end{aligned}$$ The backpropagation graph has a branching structure where gradients summate wherever the forward pass branches. (see figure: Backpropagation through time in an RNN with a loss at each timestep.)
concepts.motivation_md: Standard backpropagation cannot handle cycles in a computation graph; BPTT resolves this by treating the sequence as a deep feedforward network where each layer represents a timestep.
concepts.recap_md: - BPTT unrolls the RNN into a DAG to allow the application of standard backpropagation.

key_passage.text: To apply backpropagation to RNNs, we unroll the net for T timesteps, which creates a DAG representation of the truncated RNN, and then do backpropagation through that DAG. This is known as BPTT.

concepts.title: The Problem of Exploding and Vanishing Gradients
concepts.one_liner: RNNs suffer from vanishing or exploding gradients because the gradient computation involves a long product of matrices that can grow or shrink exponentially over time.
concepts.content: (see figure: Backpropagation through time in an RNN with a loss at each timestep.) Running an RNN for many timesteps creates very large computation graphs where gradient computation involves a series of matrix multiplies of length $\mathcal{O}(T)$. For example: $$\begin{aligned} \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}[t]}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[0]} = \frac{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{out}}[t]}{\partial \mathbf{h}_T} \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_T}{\partial \mathbf{h}_{T-1}} \cdots \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_1}{\partial \mathbf{h}_0} \frac{\partial \mathbf{h}_0}{\partial \mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[0]} \end{aligned}$$ With ReLU nonlinearities, this can result in a product of $T$ matrices $\mathbf{W}$. If values in $\mathbf{W}$ are large, the gradient will explode; if they are small, the gradient will vanish, making the system numerically unstable.
concepts.motivation_md: This problem identifies a fundamental limitation of simple RNNs, explaining why they struggle to learn long-term dependencies and motivating the development of gated architectures like LSTMs.
concepts.recap_md: - Gradients in RNNs involve a chain of matrix multiplications proportional to the sequence length.

key_passage.text: In a worst-case scenario (for numerics), suppose all the relu are active; then we have a product of T matrices W, which means the gradient is W^T (T is an exponent here, not a transpose). If values in W are large, the gradient will explode. If they are small, the gradient will vanish.

motivation.text: The gradient computation involves a series of matrix multiplies that is O(T) in length. One solution to this problem is to use RNN units that have better numerics, an example of which we will give subsequently.

concepts.title: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)
concepts.one_liner: Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) is a recurrent module designed to maintain persistent memories and avoid gradient problems using a gated cell state.
concepts.content: LSTMs are special recurrent modules designed to avoid the vanishing and exploding gradients problem. An LSTM acts as a memory controller with a cell state $\mathbf{c}$, a vector it can read from and write to, storing persistent memories. It takes a hidden state $\mathbf{h}_{t-1}$ and observation $\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[t]$ to produce an updated $\mathbf{h}_t$. Internally, subcomponents decide what to delete, write, and read. The forget gate is: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{f}_t &= \sigma(\mathbf{W}_f\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{U}_f\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[t] + \mathbf{b}_f) \end{aligned}$$ The write components are: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{i}_t &= \sigma(\mathbf{W}_i\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{U}_i\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[t] + \mathbf{b}_i)\\ \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_t &= \texttt{tanh}(\mathbf{W}_C\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{U}_c\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[t] + \mathbf{b}_c) \end{aligned}$$ The cell state update is: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{c}_t &= \mathbf{f}_t \odot \mathbf{c}_{t-1} + \mathbf{i}_t \odot \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_{t} \end{aligned}$$ Finally, the output is determined by: $$\begin{aligned} \mathbf{o}_t &= \sigma(\mathbf{W}_o\mathbf{h}_{t-1} + \mathbf{U}_o\mathbf{x}_{\texttt{in}}[t] + \mathbf{b}_o)\\ \mathbf{h}_t &= \mathbf{o}_t \odot \texttt{tanh}(\mathbf{c}_t) \end{aligned}$$ This architecture allows information to propagate through an identity connection, similar to skip connections in ResNets.
concepts.motivation_md: LSTMs were created to solve the vanishing gradient problem in standard RNNs, allowing the network to learn dependencies over much longer time intervals by protecting the cell state.
concepts.recap_md: - The cell state $\mathbf{c}_t$ allows for long-term information storage via an additive update rule.

key_passage.text: An LSTM is like a little memory controller. It has a cell state, $\mathbf{c}$, which is a vector it can read from and write to. The cell state can record memories and retrieve them as needed. The cell state plays a similar role as the hidden state, $\mathbf{h}$, from regular RNNs---both record memories---but the cell state is built to store persistent memories that can last a long time (hence the name long short-term memory).

concepts.title: Cell State
concepts.one_liner: The cell state is a vector in an LSTM that records and retrieves persistent memories over long periods.
concepts.content: An LSTM acts as a memory controller using a cell state, $\mathbf{c}$, which is a vector it can read from and write to. The cell state records memories and retrieves them as needed. While it plays a similar role to the hidden state, $\mathbf{h}$, from regular RNNs—both record memories—the cell state is specifically built to store persistent memories that can last a long time, giving the architecture its name: long short-term memory.
concepts.motivation_md: Standard RNNs struggle to maintain information over long sequences due to the vanishing gradient problem. The cell state provides a dedicated pathway for persistent information, allowing the network to remember context from many steps prior.
concepts.recap_md:
- The cell state $\mathbf{c}$ is a vector that an LSTM uses to record and retrieve information.
- It is designed to store persistent memories over much longer durations than the hidden states of standard RNNs.

concepts.title: Feedback as a Mechanism for Adaptive Systems
concepts.one_liner: Feedback via recurrent connections allows neural networks to adapt their behavior based on the consequences of previous processing.
concepts.content: Recurrent connections give neural nets the ability to maintain a persistent state representation, which can be propagated forward in time or updated in the face of incoming experience. This concept mirrors the distinction in control theory between open-loop and closed-loop control. Closed-loop control allows a controller to change its behavior based on feedback from the consequences of its previous decisions; similarly, recurrent connections allow a neural net to change its behavior based on feedback from downstream processing within the same network. Feedback is a fundamental mechanism for making systems adaptive, allowing them to become more competent the longer they run.
concepts.motivation_md: Static feedforward networks process each input in isolation. By introducing feedback through recurrence, systems can become adaptive, using their own internal state and previous outputs to refine future processing.
concepts.recap_md:
- Recurrent connections allow for persistent state representations that update with experience.
- Feedback mechanisms enable closed-loop control, making neural networks adaptive rather than static.

prereq.rationale: BPTT is specifically designed to enable the training of Recurrent Neural Networks by addressing their cyclic nature.
The problem of vanishing and exploding gradients in RNNs is a direct consequence of the long chains of matrix multiplications created by unrolling the network via BPTT.
The concept of feedback in neural networks is fundamentally implemented through the architecture of Recurrent Neural Networks.
Recurrent layers provide the specific mechanism (recurrent connections) that allows for the persistent state and feedback described.
The recurrent layer provides the formal mathematical definition for the components that constitute a Recurrent Neural Network.
LSTMs are a specialized type of recurrent neural network module.
LSTMs were specifically engineered to solve the gradient instability issues inherent in training recurrent networks.
The cell state is a fundamental component of the LSTM architecture, providing its distinctive long-term memory capability.
